sentences.text: The broad-billed moa, also known as the stout-legged or coastal moa, is an extinct species of moa endemic to New Zealand. It is the only species currently recognized within the genus Euryapteryx.
This stout bird was characterized by a blunt, downward-curving bill, wide feet, and short, thick legs.
The species showed significant sexual dimorphism, with females generally weighing about twice as much as males.
Its elongated, looped windpipe suggests it produced a deep, resonant call similar to the modern cassowary.
Eggs traditionally assigned to Euryapteryx gravis averaged 205 mm in length and 143 mm in width, while those assigned to E. curtus averaged 122 mm in length and 94 mm in width.
The species was scientifically described by British paleontologist Richard Owen in 1846, initially placing it in the genus Dinornis as D. curtus.
In 1874, German naturalist Haast described the genus Euryapteryx, designating Dinornis gravis as the type species, into which D. curtus was later included.
Analysis of gizzard remains and beak shape suggests the broad-billed moa primarily fed on leaves, fruits, and herbaceous plants, unlike the more fibrous diet of the giant moa.
The bird carried its head forward rather than upright to feed comfortably on low-lying vegetation.
The genus Euryapteryx lived from the Gelasian to the Holocene, spanning from 2.58 to 0 million years ago.
The broad-billed moa inhabited lowland environments including duneland, forest, shrubland, and grassland.

There is an ongoing debate regarding the classification of Euryapteryx gravis, with a 2009 genetic study suggesting it is a junior synonym of E. curtus, while a 2012 morphological study interpreted the differences as subspecies.
